nature-001.summary: At 6,650 kilometers, often called the longest river in the world, flowing through Sudan and Egypt into the Mediterranean.
facts: Until the Aswan High Dam was built, its annual floods enriched the fields of Egypt.
Its two main branches, the White Nile and the Blue Nile, meet at Khartoum in Sudan.

nature-002.summary: The river with the greatest discharge in the world, single-handedly pouring out about a fifth of all fresh water that flows into the oceans.
facts: It carries more water than the next seven largest rivers combined.
Not a single bridge crosses its main channel.

nature-003.summary: Asia's longest river, flowing 6,300 kilometers from the Tibetan Plateau to the sea off Shanghai.
facts: In China, it is called the Chang Jiang, meaning “Long River.”
The Three Gorges Dam across it has the largest generating capacity of any dam in the world.

nature-004.summary: A river revered by Hindus as a mother goddess, where they bathe, flowing into the Bay of Bengal.
facts: It rises at the Gangotri Glacier in the Himalayas and passes through Bangladesh before reaching the sea.
The tradition of cremation on its banks at Varanasi continues to this day.

nature-005.summary: A river that splits the continent north to south for more than 3,700 kilometers, passing New Orleans before reaching the Gulf of Mexico.
facts: Its name means “big river” in a Native American language.
Mark Twain's “Adventures of Huckleberry Finn” is set along its waters.

nature-006.summary: A river that rises in the forests of southwestern Germany and flows through or along the borders of ten countries to the Black Sea.
facts: Four capitals lie on its banks: Vienna, Bratislava, Budapest and Belgrade.
Strauss's waltz “The Beautiful Blue Danube” sings its praises.

nature-008.summary: The highest mountain range on Earth, home to ten peaks over 8,000 meters.
facts: It was pushed up by the Indian Plate colliding with the Eurasian Plate, and it still grows a few millimeters every year.
Its highest peak, Mount Everest, was remeasured in 2020 and announced at 8,848.86 meters.

nature-009.summary: A mountain range arcing 1,200 kilometers across the heart of Europe through eight countries.
facts: Its highest peak, Mont Blanc, rises over 4,800 meters.
The first Winter Olympics were held in 1924 in Chamonix, at the foot of these mountains.

nature-010.summary: The longest mountain range on land, running 8,900 kilometers north to south along the continent's western edge.
facts: The Inca built Machu Picchu on a ridge here, 2,400 meters above sea level.
Potatoes were first cultivated here before spreading to dinner tables around the world.

nature-011.summary: A mountain range stretching 4,800 kilometers from Canada to New Mexico in the United States, splitting which way the continent's rainwater flows.
facts: Denver sits at its foot at 1,600 meters above sea level, earning it the nickname “the Mile High City.”
Yellowstone National Park and Banff National Park both lie within this range.

nature-013.summary: A volcano rising right beside the Bay of Naples, whose eruption in AD 79 buried Roman towns under ash.
facts: Excavation of Pompeii, buried in its ash, began in 1748 and continues to this day.
Its most recent eruption was in 1944.

nature-014.summary: The world's largest hot desert, blanketing the entire north of the continent.
facts: Covering about 9.2 million square kilometers, it is larger than the contiguous United States.
It was once a land of grasslands and lakes.

nature-015.summary: A cold desert of gravel and rock spanning Mongolia and China.
facts: In 1923, an American expedition found a trove of fossilized dinosaur eggs here.
The yellow dust that blankets the Korean Peninsula in spring blows in from here and the surrounding deserts.

nature-016.summary: Stretching along the Pacific coast of northern Chile, the driest desert on Earth outside the poles.
facts: Some weather stations here have gone decades without a single drop of rain.
Its clear skies have drawn major observatories such as the ALMA radio telescope.

nature-017.summary: A Siberian lake that is the world's deepest at 1,642 meters and holds a fifth of the fresh surface water on Earth.
facts: The Baikal seal, one of the few freshwater seals, lives nowhere else in the world.
In winter, it freezes so thick that cars drive across it.

nature-018.summary: A group of three waterfalls on the border between the United States and Canada, where water from Lake Erie plunges on its way to Lake Ontario.
facts: In 1901, a woman became the first person to go over it in a barrel and survive.
The largest, Horseshoe Falls, is on the Canadian side, and boats take visitors right up into its spray.

nature-019.summary: At 2,500 kilometers, the continent's longest river, crossing the southeast before emptying into the sea on the south coast.
facts: The Murray–Darling Basin is Australia's most important region for irrigated farming.
So much water is drawn off that sand has been dredged from its mouth since 2002 to keep it from closing up.

nature-020.summary: A low, ancient mountain range taken as the boundary between Europe and Asia.
facts: Rich deposits of iron and copper gave rise to industrial cities such as Yekaterinburg.
Though not very high, it stretches 2,500 kilometers from north to south.

nature-021.summary: A waterfall on the border of Zambia and Zimbabwe, where the Zambezi River plunges over a cliff 1.7 kilometers wide and 108 meters high.
facts: Its local name, Mosi-oa-Tunya, means “the smoke that thunders.”
In 1855, David Livingstone became the first European to see it and named it after the British queen.

nature-022.summary: The source of the Nile, Africa's largest lake by area and the second-largest freshwater lake in the world.
facts: About half of its area belongs to Tanzania, 45 percent to Uganda and 6 percent to Kenya.
Nile perch introduced in the 1950s pushed out many native fish species.

nature-023.summary: A semi-desert in the interior of southern Africa, where grasses and trees grow on red sand.
facts: It covers most of Botswana, and the San people have lived here for 20,000 years.
After rain, grass briefly springs up and turns it into something like a grassland.

nature-024.summary: A river that crosses the equator twice before emptying into the Atlantic, ranking third in the world by discharge.
facts: Some stretches are more than 220 meters deep, making it the deepest river in the world.
Two capital cities, Kinshasa and Brazzaville, face each other across it.

nature-025.summary: A North African mountain range separating the Sahara from the Mediterranean and Atlantic coasts.
facts: It runs about 2,500 kilometers across Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia, and its highest peak, Toubkal, reaches 4,167 meters.
Legend says the Titan Atlas, who held up the sky in Greek mythology, was turned to stone and became these mountains.

nature-026.summary: Often called the oldest desert in the world, it has been arid for more than 55 million years along the Atlantic coast.
facts: At Sossusvlei, red sand dunes over 300 meters tall stand in rows.
It is home to a beetle that drinks by catching the morning fog on its back.

nature-027.summary: The lowest lake on land, nearly ten times saltier than ocean water, so bodies float on their own.
facts: Its surface lies about 440 meters below sea level.
Because the rivers feeding it are diverted for use, its level drops about 1 meter every year.

nature-028.summary: Called a sea but enclosed by land on all sides, the largest lake in the world by area.
facts: It is about 1.7 times the size of the Korean Peninsula and is bordered by five countries, including Russia and Iran.
Caviar, made from sturgeon eggs, comes from here.

nature-029.summary: A river that rises on the Tibetan Plateau and passes through six countries before reaching the South China Sea in southern Vietnam.
facts: In Vietnam, where its mouth splits into many branches, it is called the Cửu Long, meaning “Nine Dragons.”
More than half of Vietnam's rice comes from the delta at its mouth.

nature-030.summary: A river that flows 5,464 kilometers from Qinghai to the Bohai Sea, carrying so much loess that its water turns a muddy ocher.
facts: Its course has shifted dramatically many times throughout history.
Its frequent floods earned it the name “China's Sorrow.”

nature-031.summary: The world's second-highest peak at 8,611 meters, but far more treacherous, earning it the name “the Savage Mountain.”
facts: Its name was given in 1856 by a British survey team as shorthand for the second peak in the Karakoram.
The first winter ascent was not achieved until 2021.

nature-032.summary: The highest peak in the Alps, topping 4,800 meters on the border of France and Italy.
facts: Its name means “White Mountain,” and the logo of the pen maker that shares its name depicts its snowcapped summit.
In 1965, an 11.6-kilometer tunnel bored beneath it connected the two countries.

nature-033.summary: A river flowing more than 1,200 kilometers from the Alps to the North Sea, a major artery of European freight.
facts: Its castle-lined middle gorge became a World Heritage Site in 2002.
The Lorelei, the rocky cliff made famous by Heine's poem, stands on its banks.

nature-034.summary: Europe's most active volcano, perched on the island of Sicily and still erupting frequently.
facts: Records of its eruptions go back more than 3,000 years.
The volcanic soil on its slopes nurtures grapes and citrus.

nature-035.summary: Europe's longest river, flowing 3,530 kilometers entirely within Russia before emptying into the Caspian Sea.
facts: The folk song “Song of the Volga Boatmen” was sung by the laborers who hauled boats upstream.
The Battle of Stalingrad was fought on its banks.

nature-036.summary: A warm sea between Central America and the West Indies, scattered with thousands of islands.
facts: It was a stage for pirates in the 17th and 18th centuries, and the film “Pirates of the Caribbean” takes its title from it.
Its name comes from the Carib people, who lived in the region when Christopher Columbus arrived.

nature-037.summary: A river that runs 2,330 kilometers down from the Rocky Mountains, carving through rock to create the Grand Canyon.
facts: So much of its water is drawn off that since the 1960s it has rarely reached the sea.
Forty million people in seven states rely on it for water and electricity.

nature-038.summary: The northernmost of the Great Lakes and the largest freshwater lake in the world by area.
facts: About two-thirds of its area lies in the United States, with the rest in Canada.
In 1975, the freighter Edmund Fitzgerald sank in it during a storm.

nature-039.summary: An Alaskan peak that, at 6,190 meters, is the highest in North America.
facts: Its Native name, Denali, was restored in 2015, but in 2025 the U.S. government changed it back to McKinley.
Its rise from base to summit is greater than that of Mount Everest.

nature-040.summary: A volcano just 70 kilometers from Mexico City that is still puffing out smoke.
facts: Its name means “smoking mountain” in Nahuatl.
Major eruptions sometimes force nearby airports to close.

nature-041.summary: Some 270 cascades plunging over a cliff edge 2.7 kilometers long.
facts: They straddle the border between Brazil and Argentina.
The deepest part is called the “Devil's Throat.”

nature-042.summary: The world's largest and most biodiverse tropical forest, spanning nine countries and territories, including Brazil.
facts: One in ten known species lives here.
About 60% of the forest lies within Brazil.

nature-043.summary: A lake on an Andean plateau 3,812 meters above sea level, the highest of all lakes navigable by large ships.
facts: Peru and Bolivia share the lake between them.
People live on islands woven from reeds.

nature-044.summary: South America's second-longest river after the Amazon River, rising in southern Brazil and flowing south.
facts: The Itaipu Dam, built jointly by Brazil and Paraguay, harnesses the river, and the two countries share its power.
It joins the Uruguay River to form the Río de la Plata estuary.

nature-045.summary: The deepest place on Earth's seafloor, where the lowest point, the Challenger Deep, plunges past 10,900 meters.
facts: Even Mount Everest turned upside down would leave over 2,000 meters to spare.
The bathyscaphe Trieste reached the bottom in 1960, and James Cameron did so in 2012.

nature-046.summary: A chain of mountains stretching 3,500 kilometers along the east coast and blocking rain clouds.
facts: Even its highest peak, Mount Kosciuszko, is a modest 2,228 meters.
The Blue Mountains near Sydney are part of the chain.

nature-047.summary: The world's second-largest island after Greenland, split roughly in half between two countries.
facts: More than 800 languages are spoken here.
Though it lies near the equator, a few glaciers survive on its high mountains, but they are on the verge of disappearing.

nature-048.summary: An island cut off 240 kilometers across the sea south of the mainland, where unique animals have survived.
facts: The Tasmanian devil, a pouched carnivore, lives in the wild almost only on this island.
About 11,700 years ago, rising seas created the Bass Strait and separated it from the mainland.

nature-049.summary: Called Aoraki in Māori, the 3,724-meter summit is the highest peak of the Southern Alps on the South Island.
facts: A 1991 rockslide knocked 10 meters off its summit.
Before conquering Mount Everest, Hillary climbed its south ridge in 1948.

nature-050.summary: Australia's largest desert, where red sand dunes and gravel plains stretch more than 700 kilometers from east to west.
facts: In the 1950s, the United Kingdom carried out nuclear tests at Maralinga in this desert.
Explorer Ernest Giles, who first crossed it in 1875, named it after Queen Victoria.
